title: A Spilling Galaxy
caption: The WIYN 3.5-meter Telescope under the Milky Way, Kitt Peak National Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way rises from the horizon behind the Wisconsin-Indiana-Yale-NOIRLab (WIYN) 3.5-meter Telescope, which seems to be watching it. A reddish airglow, a natural phenomenon, tints the horizon. The telescope stands at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO).

KPNO lies on the Tohono O'odham Nation, in the Arizona-Sonoran Desert. The clear view of part of our galaxy's plane shows why the site suits the study of faint objects. Light pollution is low, the air is dry, and the sky is darker than magnitude 20. Magnitude is the astronomers' scale of brightness, and higher numbers mean fainter light.

Those conditions have let researchers in the WIYN Consortium observe galaxies, nebulas, exoplanets and many other targets. They work with the 3.5-meter telescope and with its smaller sibling, the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope.

understand.summary: A night landscape photograph by R. Sparks. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and airglow would look fainter in person.

explore: The credit names the photographer as R. Sparks. Airglow is faint light given off by Earth's upper atmosphere itself, which is why it can tint the sky even at a dark site.
alt: The WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak with the Milky Way spilling up from a reddish horizon.
